title: Precision, accuracy and resolution

learning_outcomes.text: understand the distinction between precision and accuracy

prior_knowledge_summary: A systematic error shifts repeated measurements consistently in the same direction.
A zero error is a systematic error revealed when an instrument gives a non-zero reading for a true zero input.
A random error changes unpredictably between readings and produces scatter.
Repeated readings and a mean can reduce the effect of random error, but repetition alone does not remove a systematic offset.
new_learning: Precision is judged from the agreement among repeated measurements, indicated by their spread or range.
Accuracy is judged by closeness to the true value.
Instrument resolution is the smallest change that an instrument can distinguish.
High precision, high accuracy and fine resolution are different properties and none guarantees the others.
not_yet_taught: Applications belonging to later Physics topics.

visual_planning.reason: Six distinct visuals establish the opening measurement puzzle, define spread and closeness separately, compare repeated sets numerically, show instrument resolution, correct the fine-resolution misconception and finish with a three-question decision route.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Which group measured the reference length better?
content: A reference block has a true length of 12.50 cm. Group A records 12.83 cm, 12.82 cm, 12.83 cm and 12.82 cm. Group B records 12.44 cm, 12.56 cm, 12.49 cm and 12.51 cm.
Group A's readings almost repeat one another, but they sit away from the true value. Group B's readings spread farther apart, yet their mean is 12.50 cm.
There is no single word meaning 'good measurement'. We need separate language for agreement among repeats, closeness to truth and the smallest change the instrument can show.

figure.purpose: Create a contradiction between a tight displaced cluster and a wider cluster centred on the true value
figure.brief: Draw a rectangular white-paper teacher sketch with a horizontal length scale and a green reference line at 12.50 cm. Put four tightly grouped blue marks near 12.82 to 12.83 cm and four orange marks from 12.44 to 12.56 cm. Label only group A, group B and true value. Do not use the words precision, accuracy or resolution.
figure.alt_text: One group of repeated lengths is tightly clustered away from the true value while another wider group is centred on it.

blocks.title: Precision asks how closely repeats agree
content: Definition to learn: precision is the degree of agreement among repeated measurements, indicated by their spread or range.
Find the range by subtracting the smallest reading from the largest. Group A has range 12.83 cm - 12.82 cm = 0.01 cm. Group B has range 12.56 cm - 12.44 cm = 0.12 cm.
Group A is more precise because its repeated values have the smaller range. This conclusion compares readings with one another. It does not use the true value.
One isolated reading cannot show agreement among repeats. Several measurements are needed before precision can be judged from their spread.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: the degree of agreement among repeated measurements, indicated by their spread or range

figure.purpose: Make range the visible evidence for comparing precision
figure.brief: Create a colourful hand-drawn two-row range comparison. Show group A from 12.82 to 12.83 cm with a short blue bracket labelled range 0.01 cm. Show group B from 12.44 to 12.56 cm with a longer orange bracket labelled range 0.12 cm. Add the question 'Which repeats agree more closely?'.
figure.alt_text: A short range of 0.01 centimetres is compared with a wider range of 0.12 centimetres.

blocks.title: Accuracy asks how close a result is to truth
content: Definition to learn: accuracy is the closeness of a measured value to the true value of the quantity.

When repeated readings are used, their mean can be treated as the measured value for the set. Group A has mean (12.83 + 12.82 + 12.83 + 12.82) cm / 4 = 12.825 cm, which is about 0.33 cm above 12.50 cm.
Group B has mean (12.44 + 12.56 + 12.49 + 12.51) cm / 4 = 12.50 cm. Its mean is equal to the true value, so this set gives the more accurate result.
Accuracy compares a measured value with truth. Precision compares repeated values with one another. A set can therefore be precise but not accurate.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: the closeness of a measured value to the true value of the quantity

figure.purpose: Separate comparison with the true value from comparison among repeated readings
figure.brief: Draw a rectangular teacher-sketch calculation card. Show a green true-value post at 12.50 cm, a blue group A mean at 12.825 cm and an orange group B mean at 12.50 cm. Use arrows labelled distance from true value. Keep both mean calculations visible and do not add uncertainty notation.
figure.alt_text: The mean of group B coincides with the true value while the mean of group A lies above it.

blocks.title: Resolution belongs to the instrument
content: Definition to learn: instrument resolution is the smallest change in a quantity that a measuring instrument can distinguish, usually set by its smallest scale division.
A ruler marked every 1 mm has resolution 1 mm. If two lengths differ by only 0.2 mm, this ruler cannot show that change reliably as a separate scale step.

A digital balance that changes from 6.42 g to 6.43 g in steps of 0.01 g has resolution 0.01 g. The last displayed digit tells us the smallest displayed change, not whether the reading is close to the true mass.

Choose an instrument whose measuring range includes the object and whose resolution is fine enough for the change that matters. A micrometer may suit a thin wire, while calipers may suit a much longer object that must still be read more finely than a metre rule allows.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: the smallest change in a quantity that a measuring instrument can distinguish, usually set by its smallest scale division

figure.purpose: Show resolution as the smallest visible instrument step
figure.brief: Create a rectangular colourful hand-drawn comparison with a ruler segment marked every 1 mm and a digital balance changing from 6.42 g to 6.43 g. Highlight one smallest step on each instrument with a coloured bracket. Label resolution 1 mm and resolution 0.01 g. Keep accuracy and precision labels absent.
figure.alt_text: A ruler's smallest one millimetre division and a balance's 0.01 gram display step are highlighted.

blocks.title: More digits do not guarantee a better measurement
content: It feels natural to trust the instrument with more decimal places. More digits can show finer resolution, but the reading may still contain a systematic offset or the repeats may still scatter.

Imagine a balance with resolution 0.01 g that reads +0.40 g when empty. It can distinguish small changes, yet every uncorrected mass is shifted upward. Its fine resolution does not make those values accurate.

Imagine instead that readings jump among 8.21 g, 8.34 g, 8.16 g and 8.29 g. The balance displays hundredths of a gram, but the repeated values have a range of 0.18 g. Fine resolution has not guaranteed high precision for this procedure.
Ask three separate questions: How close are the repeats? How close is the result to truth? What smallest change can the instrument distinguish?

figure.purpose: Break the mistaken link between many displayed digits and trustworthy measurements
figure.brief: Draw a colourful two-panel teacher sketch. Left panel: a digital balance with 0.01 g steps but an empty reading of +0.40 g, with a red shared-offset arrow. Right panel: the same 0.01 g display style showing four widely spread readings, with an orange range bracket of 0.18 g. Add the caption 'fine steps, separate quality questions'.
figure.alt_text: A fine-resolution balance can still have a fixed zero offset or widely scattered repeated readings.

blocks.title: Judge a measurement without mixing the three ideas
content: A thermometer has resolution 0.1 degrees Celsius. A reference temperature is 25.0 degrees Celsius. Four readings are 25.6, 25.5, 25.6 and 25.5 degrees Celsius.
First judge precision from repeats. The range is 25.6 - 25.5 = 0.1 degrees Celsius, so the readings agree closely and are precise.
Next judge accuracy from truth. Their mean is (25.6 + 25.5 + 25.6 + 25.5) / 4 = 25.55 degrees Celsius, which is about 0.6 degrees Celsius above the true value. The result is not accurate.

Finally state resolution from the instrument. It is 0.1 degrees Celsius, the smallest displayed change. The pattern is consistent with a systematic offset from the previous lesson. A calibration or zero check is needed; taking more similarly shifted readings will not restore accuracy.
Independent check: the mean must lie between the smallest and largest readings, and 25.55 lies between 25.5 and 25.6.

figure.purpose: Model a complete precision, accuracy, resolution and prior-error diagnosis in a fixed order
figure.brief: Create a rectangular annotated teacher-sketch workflow. Show the four thermometer readings, a range card 0.1 degrees Celsius, a mean card 25.55 degrees Celsius beside a true-value card 25.0 degrees Celsius, and a scale step labelled 0.1 degrees Celsius. Join them with numbered arrows labelled repeats, truth and instrument. End with a small calibration-check icon.
figure.alt_text: Four thermometer readings are assessed in turn for range, distance from a true value and smallest instrument step.

blocks.title: Use three questions in the right order
content: For precision, compare repeated readings with one another. A small spread or range means close agreement; a large spread means low precision.
For accuracy, compare the measured value, or a representative mean, with the true value. A close result is accurate; a displaced result is not.
For instrument resolution, inspect the smallest scale division or display step. Finer resolution allows smaller changes to be distinguished, but it does not by itself guarantee precision or accuracy.

Connect this language to the previous lesson without replacing it. Random error tends to widen the spread and limit precision. A systematic offset can reduce accuracy while leaving a set tightly grouped. The next lesson will calculate and combine uncertainties, which has not been taught here.
